notes: Cambridge primate research Green Belt permission; Bushell policy approach upheld despite university withdrawal.

enrichment.short_title: Cambridge primate research Green Belt planning challenge
key_facts: The Secretary of State granted planning permission for a Cambridge University behavioural neuroscience research building in the Green Belt at Huntingdon Road.
The National Anti-Vivisection Society challenged the decision, arguing pre-determination, missing Coalition witness statements, and need for a use-limiting condition.
The university later announced it would not proceed for financial reasons, but the permission ran with the land and remained challengeable.
Lord Sainsbury ministerial letters were relied on to establish national importance and very special circumstances.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a called-in planning appeal decision granting Green Belt development permission.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no error of law in treating ministerial letters as government policy under Bushell; condition and procedural fairness grounds rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Government policy promoting nationally important research centres may properly be weighed in Green Belt very-special-circumstances balancing; a local inquiry is not the forum to re-debate that policy (Bushell); absent party request, the Secretary of State need not impose a limiting use condition (Top Deck Holdings).
legal_issues: Whether Lord Sainsbury letters amounted to government policy
Application of Bushell to national scientific need evidence
Procedural fairness where witness statements omitted from Secretary of State papers
Whether a condition limiting use to animal research was required
linked_authorities: Bushell v Secretary of State for the Environment [1981] AC 75
Top Deck Holdings Ltd v Secretary of State for the Environment [1991] JPL 961
Marie Finlay v Secretary of State for the Environment [1983] JPL 802

confidence.notes: Core Bushell and condition principles are clearly decided; costs discussion is peripheral.

notes: Roof-space lease forfeiture waiver and unreasonable withholding of assignment consent; Ashworth Frazer principles applied.

enrichment.short_title: Penthouse lease: waiver of breach and consent to assign
key_facts: ACP held a 1005-year roof-space lease at Albert Court to develop penthouses; CHAPS held the overriding reversion.
Development was incomplete; CHAPS served section 146 notice but later waived breach by affirming the lease and accepting rent.
First Penthouse as chargee assigned the lease to Mr Tamimi after CHAPS refused consent unless he assumed preliminary agreement obligations.
Lightman J held waiver effective and consent unreasonably withheld; CHAPS appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from preliminary issues trial on waiver of covenant breach and reasonableness of landlord's refusal of licence to assign.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; breach was once-and-for-all and waived; refusal of consent unreasonable under Ashworth Frazer principles.
enrichment.ratio: A covenant to complete development works expeditiously by an agreed date is a once-and-for-all obligation (Farimani), not continuing; collateral interests in preliminary agreement profit-sharing are not grounds to refuse assignment; the 1999 Deed of Priorities precluded CHAPS from objecting on that basis.
legal_issues: Continuing versus once-and-for-all breach of development covenant
Waiver of right to forfeit by affirming lease
Reasonableness of withholding consent to assign
Relevance of landlord's collateral commercial interests
linked_authorities: Ashworth Frazer Ltd v Gloucester City Council [2001] 1 WLR 2180
Farimani v Gates [1984] 2 EGLR 66
Midland Bank Trust Co Ltd v Hett, Stubbs & Kemp [1979] Ch 384

confidence.notes: Preliminary issue findings and appeal outcome are explicit; relief from forfeiture not decided.

notes: ECRC disclosure appeal allowed; section 115(7) 'might be relevant' standard and limited pre-disclosure fairness.

enrichment.short_title: Enhanced criminal record certificate disclosure challenge
key_facts: X, a social worker, faced ECRC disclosure of unproven indecent exposure allegations after charges were discontinued following failed covert ID.
Wall J quashed disclosure as substantively and procedurally unfair; chief constable appealed.
The Deputy Chief Constable approved disclosure after risk assessment of threats-to-rape allegations and interview responses.
X had applied for the certificate for a post caring for vulnerable persons.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by chief constable against quashing of Police Act 1997 section 115(7) enhanced criminal record certificate disclosure decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; quashing orders set aside; claim dismissed; leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 115(7) the chief officer must disclose information he opines might be relevant unless good reason not to; the statutory scheme displaces ex parte Thorpe presumption against disclosure; pre-disclosure representations are not generally required where the applicant initiated the process and may correct the certificate under section 117.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of non-conviction ECRC disclosure under section 115(7)
Article 8 proportionality of disclosure
Procedural fairness and opportunity to make representations
Application of ex parte Thorpe and Re LM principles
linked_authorities: R v Chief Constable of North Wales Police, ex parte Thorpe [1999] QB 396
R v A Local Authority in the Midlands, ex parte LM [2000] 1 FLR 612

confidence.notes: Appeal outcome and statutory analysis are clear; Article 8(1) engagement left open by Mummery LJ.

notes: Section 39 CJA 1991 recall representations: one referral plus material-change exception; claims dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Licence recall and further section 39 representations
key_facts: Francis and Clarke, short-term prisoners recalled on licence, made initial section 39(3) written representations referred to the Parole Board.
After acquittal on charges that featured in recall decisions, solicitors sent further representations which the Secretary of State refused to re-refer.
Francis had been released again before judgment; Clarke remained in custody.
The Secretary of State argued one referral only, alternatively re-referral only on material change of circumstances.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Conjoined judicial review of refusal to refer further written representations after Parole Board rejection of initial section 39 recall representations.
enrichment.outcome: Claims dismissed; section 39 allows further representations only where a material change of circumstances gives realistic prospect of a different view; Secretary of State may filter threshold.
enrichment.ratio: Section 39 is protective of recall decisions, not open-ended review of continuing detention; unlimited re-referrals would distort the scheme; Interpretation Act section 12 permits repeat performance on occasion requiring it, satisfied only by material change relevant to recall such as subsequent acquittal.
legal_issues: Whether section 39 permits multiple sets of written representations
Whether Parole Board is functus officio after first reference
Material change of circumstances test for re-referral
Who decides whether further representations warrant referral
linked_authorities: R v Parole Board, ex parte Watson [1996] 1 WLR 906
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Robinson (unreported, 29 July 1999)
R v Ealing LBC, ex parte McBain [1985] 1 WLR 1351
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Onibyo [1996] 2 WLR 496

confidence.notes: Statutory interpretation holding is explicit; individual merits of second representations not adjudicated.

notes: Coffee-machine copyright interim applications: service out upheld, authorisation amendment refused, stay refused.

enrichment.short_title: Senseo coffee software copyright: jurisdiction and stay
key_facts: Philips sued Salton Europe in England for UK copyright infringement in One:One coffee-maker control software allegedly copied from Senseo software.
Electrical & Electronics manufactured the machines in Hong Kong; parallel proceedings existed there and in the US.
SHK joined EE as Part 20 defendant; EE challenged jurisdiction and sought stay pending Hong Kong copyright trial.
Philips pursued summary judgment while SE offered undertakings not to distribute accused machines pending that application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interim applications on service out of jurisdiction, Part 20 amendment for authorisation, and stay of English proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Service out on EE upheld as proper Part 20 party; authorisation amendment refused as unarguable; stay refused; English summary judgment may proceed.
enrichment.ratio: A foreign Part 20 defendant need not be co-liable on the same cause of action if necessary/proper to resolve connected issues (United Film Distribution); supplying goods with knowledge of destination does not authorise UK infringement without control (CBS v Amstrad); claimant may prioritise English proceedings absent compelling reasons for Hong Kong first.
legal_issues: CPR Part 6.20(3A) service out for Part 20 claims
Authorisation of copyright infringement by manufacturer
Stay pending foreign copyright proceedings
Effect of Brussels Regulation on case management stay
linked_authorities: United Film Distributors Ltd v Chabria [2001] EWCA Civ 416
CBS Songs Ltd v Amstrad Consumer Electronics Plc [1988] 1 AC 1013
Pensher Security Door Co Ltd v Sunderland City Council [2000] RPC 249

notes: Long Bahl v Law Society race and sex discrimination appeal; Court of Appeal dismissed all grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Law Society vice-president race and sex discrimination appeal
key_facts: Dr Bahl, a black Asian solicitor and former EOC chair, was elected Law Society vice-president in 1999.
Staff complaints about her management led to investigation, suspension, censure and a special general meeting.
An employment tribunal found race and sex discrimination by the Law Society, Robert Sayer and Jane Betts.
The EAT reversed those findings; Dr Bahl appealed on multiple grounds including procedural unfairness and unconscious bias.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal allowing respondents' appeals against tribunal discrimination findings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; renewed permission refused; House of Lords permission refused.
enrichment.ratio: The EAT's reversal of discrimination findings was upheld: the disciplinary process, though harsh, was not shown to be tainted by race or sex discrimination; alleged procedural defects and differential treatment did not establish unlawful discrimination on appeal.
legal_issues: Direct and indirect race discrimination in professional disciplinary process
Sex discrimination in treatment of elected Law Society officer
Procedural fairness of investigation and suspension
Unconscious bias and comparator treatment of previous office holders

confidence.notes: Very long judgment; outcome and core discrimination issue clear but detailed ground-by-ground analysis is extensive.

notes: Import quota 'related persons' control finding upheld; public interest petition dismissed on undertakings.

enrichment.short_title: China import quota scheme and public interest winding-up
key_facts: BDT and KTA operated a scheme recruiting individuals to form Quota Companies applying for non-traditional EU import licences for Chinese footwear and ceramics.
The DTI investigated, revoked many licences and presented section 124A public interest winding-up petitions.
David Richards J found Quota Companies were related persons under Article 143 control test but dismissed petitions on undertakings to cease the scheme.
The Court of Appeal upheld control findings and rejected challenge to conditional undertakings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Companies Court decision on public interest winding-up petitions conditional on undertakings ceasing unlawful quota scheme.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; control finding upheld; undertakings not set aside; 75% costs order below upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Quota Companies were operationally controlled by BDT/KTA despite nominal shareholder ownership, breaching related-persons rules; winding-up was not just and equitable once undertakings ensured scheme cessation, but declaratory proceedings would have been preferable to section 124A petitions.
legal_issues: Meaning of control under Article 143(1)(f) for related persons
Lawfulness of multi-company non-traditional quota applications
Appropriate use of section 124A public interest winding-up
Enforceability of undertakings given to avoid winding up
linked_authorities: Re Supporting Link [2004] EWHC 523 (Ch)
Re Walter L Jacob Ltd [1989] 5 BCC 244
Snook v London and West Riding Investments Ltd [1967] 2 QB 786

notes: CCRC referral on cocaine contamination and sections 34/36 directions; appeals dismissed after fresh expert evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Drug import conspiracy: banknote contamination and silence directions

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Ronald and Sylvia Benn were convicted in 1997 of conspiracy to evade prohibition on importing Class A drugs after repeated Hull-Rotterdam trips and £63,000 cash contaminated with cocaine.
Forensic evidence from Dr Sleeman compared note contamination levels with MSA Ltd databases; customs also found cocaine in safe, vacuum cleaner and BMW.
The CCRC referred the case citing Mr Bottomley's critique of methodology and database validity, and alleged summing-up defects on sections 34 and 36.
Fresh expert evidence was admitted at the appeal hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by reference of Criminal Cases Review Commission against 1997 convictions after earlier leave refusal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; fresh expert evidence did not undermine safe convictions; sections 34/36 directions adequate in context.
enrichment.ratio: Database limitations did not negate overwhelming circumstantial case and striking contamination levels (Compton); judge's sections 34/36 direction, though not in modern form, sufficed where case to answer was abundant and real reason for silence was for jury; misstatement of Dr Sleeman's evidence not material.
legal_issues: Admissibility and weight of mass spectrometry cocaine contamination evidence
Validity of comparison databases for banknote contamination
Adequacy of sections 34 and 36 silence directions
Risk of innocent contamination in forensic sampling
linked_authorities: R v Compton [2002] EWCA Crim 2835
Condron v UK (2001) 31 EHRR 1
R v Betts and Hall [2001] 2 Cr App R 257

notes: Turkish notary service invalid for foreign proceedings; default judgment set aside; CPR 3.10 and 6.9 refused.

enrichment.short_title: Turkish service of proceedings and default judgment set aside

statutes_considered.title: Hague Convention on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents in Civil or Commercial Matters 1965

key_facts: Shiblaq obtained default judgment against Sadikoglu after purported service in Turkey by a notary attaching notice to a shipyard door in September 2001.
Conflicting Turkish expert evidence on whether notaries may serve foreign proceedings; Turkey had registered an objection under Hague Convention Article 10.
The claimant argued Article 15 permitted default judgment if domestic Turkish service methods were used; defendant sought set-aside and refused CPR 3.10/6.9 relief.
This was the second judgment following Colman J's July 2003 first judgment on related service issues.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court application to set aside default judgment after dispute over validity of service out of the jurisdiction in Turkey.
enrichment.outcome: Default judgment set aside under CPR 13.2; service held invalid; applications under CPR 3.10 and CPR 6.9 refused.
enrichment.ratio: Article 15 of the Hague Convention sets minimum standards for default judgment after Convention service methods, not a route to substitute domestic Turkish service for impermissible foreign service where Turkey objected to Article 10; CPR 3.10 and CPR 6.9 cannot retrospectively validate service that circumvented the Convention or impose a fictional duty to acknowledge service.
legal_issues: Validity of direct notary service of foreign proceedings in Turkey
Construction of Hague Convention Articles 10 and 15
Whether CPR 3.10 can cure defective service out
Whether CPR 6.9 can dispense with service to sustain default judgment
linked_authorities: Elmes v Hygrade Food Products plc [2001] EWCA Civ 121
Anderton v Clwyd County Council (No 2) [2002] 1 WLR 3174
Knauf UK v British Gypsum Ltd [2002] 1 WLR 907
Bas Capital Funding Corporation [2004] 1 Lloyd's Rep 652

notes: BATCo privilege appeal on Minnesota Consent Judgment; waiver and mootness issues are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Voluntary waiver of legal privilege after Minnesota tobacco settlement documents released
key_facts: BATCo appealed a Commercial Court declaration that it had voluntarily waived privilege in documents placed in the Minnesota Depository under the Minnesota Consent Judgment.
The documents became publicly available after court approval despite BATCo's objections to disclosure.
Moore-Bick J held BATCo voluntarily accepted the risk that documents might enter the public domain when agreeing to the MCJ.
The USA contended the appeal was moot after Mr Foyle's examination had concluded.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited appeal from a Commercial Court directions ruling on privilege waiver before examination of a solicitor witness under a US Letter of Request.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; declaration set aside; privilege not voluntarily waived because disclosure followed court compulsion overriding BATCo's objections.
enrichment.ratio: Under English law, agreeing to a consent judgment machinery that allows a court to approve public release of documents does not amount to voluntary waiver of privilege where the party objected and disclosure occurred only after court approval; foreign court rulings on waiver under other legal systems do not bind English courts and issue estoppel does not apply where the foreign decision was on different law.
legal_issues: Whether BATCo voluntarily waived legal privilege in MCJ documents
Construction and effect of the Minnesota Consent Judgment under English law
Whether the appeal was moot
Whether issue estoppel arose from Judge Kessler's US ruling
linked_authorities: Paragon Finance plc v Freshfields [1999] 1 WLR 1183
Bourns Inc v Raychem Corp [1999] 3 All ER 154
R (Rusbridger) v Attorney General [2004] 1 AC 357
The Good Challenger [2004] 1 Lloyd's Rep 67
